Two hands, moving together.
But only the right one is really moving.
After a stroke, one hand often moves far less than the other.
In mirror therapy, a mirror hides that hand, and shows the stronger hand's reflection in its place.
A 2018 review of sixty-two trials found moderate-quality evidence that it improves movement after stroke.
Mirror Hand is that mirror, in a headset.
First, you hold up the hand that moves more easily.
Open and close, slowly, and try to move the weaker hand along with what you see.
Thumb to each fingertip. Every touch rings a lantern.
Then reach for pairs of fireflies, which stay close to where you first held your hand.
Then the mirror switches off,
and the weaker hand tries on its own.
Then it asks one question: how did that feel?
At the end, it shows how far that hand opened, measured against your own stronger hand.
After the first two sessions, each one is planned from your last few.
After two good days, there is a little more, and the start page says why.
After pain, the next session is shorter, with nearer targets.
And the finger that opened least gets extra touches.
These are plain rules on the headset, guided by rehabilitation research. Nothing is uploaded.
Underneath, the headset tracks twenty-five joints in the moving hand.
Every frame, each joint is reflected across the middle of the body, and the other hand is drawn from those reflections.
It also fits the narrower view of Meta VR Glasses, where you look at a button and pinch to press it.
Mirror Hand. A three-minute daily practice, seated, hands only.
It is not a medical device, and has not yet been tested on a headset, or with patients.
